Time_Annotation: On September 27, convection increased near the center, and the depression strengthened into Tropical Storm Kate. It also states that 'in Atlantic Canada, ... officials advised residents' and that warnings were issued for Newfoundland (Canada). Further, it mentions that the cyclone 'reattained hurricane-force winds while passing southeast of Greenland', 'turned eastward, passing a short distance south of Iceland', and that 'the extratropical remnant of Hurricane Kate produced winds of up to 70 mph (110 km/h) in northern Scotland'.
Main_Event_Annotation: The text explains that the system strengthened into Tropical Storm Kate on September 27 and later reached hurricane status (with a well-defined eye and peak intensity of 125 mph on October 4), confirming its categorization as a tropical cyclone.
Hazards_Annotation: The article emphasizes wind hazards, noting that despite periods of weakening, Kate produced significant winds—including sustained winds of up to 40 mph (64 km/h) at Cape Race, Newfoundland, and hurricane-force winds (up to 70 mph or 110 km/h) in northern Scotland—which are the primary hazard associated with a tropical storm/cyclone.

Time_Annotation: On May 25, 2009, an area of low pressure developed along the tail-end of a decaying cold front near the northern Bahamas. By May 28, deep convection developed across a small area over the low-pressure system, leading to the National Hurricane Center classifying the system as Tropical Depression One. Late on May 29, the system degenerated into a remnant low.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The precursor to the system brought scattered rainfall and increased winds to parts of the North Carolina coastline.

Hazards_Annotation: The text cites increased winds along the North Carolina coastline with sustained winds of 15 mph and gusts up to 23 mph, indicating a wind hazard.

As a result, mandatory evacuations were ordered south of U.S. Route 98 and around the Sopchoppy River.

Time_Annotation: The text states, 'Throughout June 25, an intense complex of thunderstorms developed to the north of Debby's center…' and also notes that in Apalachicola, events were observed on 'June 24' (e.g., 6.03 inches of rainfall and bridge closures due to high winds), indicating the event spanned from June 24 to June 25.

A man drowned near Lake Dorr in Lake County after his canoe capsized along a river in Ocala National Forest.

Another person drowned on a river in Polk County after his canoe capsized; however, it is unknown whether or not his death was attributable to Debby.
Emergency managers ordered mandatory evacuations for 14,000–20,000 people along the Anclote and Pithlachascotee Rivers in Pasco County as the rivers rose dramatically.

Time_Annotation: On 5 April, the Bureau of Meteorology reported that Tropical Low 22U had formed in the far northeastern Gulf of Carpentaria. The low eventually dissipated by 05:00 UTC on 15 April over the Great Sandy Desert.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The article refers to impacts along the Northern Territory coastline (near the Arafura Sea), landfall near Onslow in Western Australia, and effects in regions such as the Arnhem District and Top End, all of which are in Australia.
Main_Event_Annotation: The text describes Tropical Low 22U as a tropical system that, despite not being upgraded to a full tropical cyclone, exhibited behaviors (such as organized spiral banding and wind patterns) consistent with the Tropical Storm/Cyclone category from the association table.
Hazards_Annotation: The article details sustained moderate to heavy rainfall (indicating a flood hazard) in areas like the Arnhem District and also documents gusty winds – for instance, 10‐minute sustained winds up to 63 km/h on Varanus Island and gusts up to 87 km/h near Onslow – which point to a wind hazard.

Time_Annotation: On 21 April, as the low began to deepen, the system embedded within the trough was classified by the Bureau of Meteorology as a tropical low, while located southwest of the Indonesian island of Sumatra. Having lost its structure, the Bureau of Meteorology indicated that the storm had dissipated as a tropical low by 06:00 UTC on 26 April.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The article notes heavy precipitation over the central‐eastern Indian Ocean with significant rainfall in the region of the Cocos (Keeling) Islands—a populated Australian external territory—and indicates that the tropical low’s track brought it within a few hundred kilometres of the Cocos Islands, where sustained winds were recorded at Cocos Islands Airport.
Main_Event_Annotation: The system was classified as a tropical low (and later as a tropical depression) with forecasts suggesting potential tropical cyclone development, aligning it with the Tropical Storm/Cyclone category as per the association table.
Hazards_Annotation: The text reports strong winds at Cocos Islands Airport (with sustained winds of 59 km/h and gusts up to 76 km/h) and describes heavy precipitation and moderate rainfall over the islands, which correspond to the wind and flood hazards associated with a Tropical Storm/Cyclone.

Time_Annotation: The tropical low was upgraded to a Category 1 tropical cyclone on the Australian scale at 03:00 UTC on 9 May by the Indonesian Agency for Meteorology, Climatology and Geophysics, and Lili was downgraded to a tropical low at 12:00 UTC on 10 May and dissipated by 06:00 UTC on 11 May upon making landfall in northern East Timor.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Lili dissipated by 06:00 UTC on 11 May upon making landfall in northern East Timor.
Main_Event_Annotation: Located just inside the area of responsibility of TCWC Jakarta upon reaching tropical cyclone status, the system was officially named Lili by the BMKG.
Hazards_Annotation: Soon afterwards, the JTWC followed suit, indicating that the storm's sustained winds had increased to the equivalent of tropical-storm-force on the Saffir–Simpson hurricane wind scale (SSHWS).
